questions.text:
Complete the sentences.

Batch jobs wait in a job [[1]]. The input data is often [[2]] before processing. The output for slow printers is placed in a queue — this is called [[3]].

questions.title: What an RTOS is
questions.text: Which statement best describes a **real-time operating system**?

options.content: An OS that processes inputs and responds within a guaranteed time limit to control a physical process
An OS that runs jobs overnight without any user interaction
An OS that manages user accounts and shared printers on a server
An OS that shows the real date and time on the screen

scheme.mark_scheme: A
scheme.explanation: The key idea is a guaranteed deadline (deterministic response).

questions.title: Fast or on time?
questions.text: The main aim of a real-time operating system is the fastest possible **average** speed.

scheme.mark_scheme: False.
scheme.explanation: Its aim is to meet every deadline — a predictable (deterministic) response, not the best average.

questions.title: Systems that need an RTOS
questions.text: Select the **three** systems that need a real-time operating system.

options.content: A car's anti-lock braking system
Printing a school's end-of-term reports overnight
A pacemaker
An industrial welding robot
A shared folder on a school server

scheme.mark_scheme: A and C and D. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.
scheme.explanation: Reports overnight = batch; shared folder = network OS.

questions.title: Pre-emptive scheduling
questions.text:
Complete the sentences.

A sensor sends an [[1]] to the processor when an event needs attention. In an RTOS the task with the highest [[2]] runs first and can stop (pre-empt) a less important task. Because the response time is predictable, an RTOS is called [[3]].

scheme.mark_scheme: (1) interrupt (2) priority (3) deterministic
scheme.explanation: Interrupt → highest-priority task runs → deterministic response.

questions.title: What a NOS is
questions.text: What is a **network operating system**?

options.content: An OS that controls a machine within strict deadlines
An OS, usually on a server, that manages a network's users and shared resources such as files and printers
A program that connects a computer to the Internet
An OS that groups similar jobs and runs them at night

scheme.explanation: A NOS gives central control for large networks; peer-to-peer suits small, cheap networks.

questions.title: Why use groups
questions.text: A NOS administrator gives access rights to **groups** (e.g. Grade 12) rather than to each user separately. Why?

options.content: Groups make the server's processor faster
A new user gets all the correct rights just by being added to the group, so management is quicker and more consistent
Users in a group do not need passwords
Groups stop the server from being backed up

scheme.mark_scheme: B

questions.title: What batch processing is
questions.text: Which statement describes a **batch processing** operating system?

options.content: Similar jobs are grouped and run one after another automatically, without user interaction, often at a scheduled time
Every input gets a response within milliseconds
Many users share files and printers on a network
The user types commands and sees each result immediately

scheme.mark_scheme: A

questions.title: Advantages of batch processing
questions.text: Select the **two** advantages of batch processing.

options.content: Large volumes of similar data are processed efficiently
Results are available immediately
Jobs can run at off-peak times without an operator
Users can change a job while it is running

scheme.mark_scheme: A and C. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.
scheme.explanation: Results are delayed and jobs cannot be changed while running — those are disadvantages.

questions.text: Which task is **not** suitable for batch processing?

options.content: Producing monthly payslips
Printing quarterly water bills
Checking a customer's balance when they withdraw cash from an ATM
Processing the day's card payments overnight

scheme.mark_scheme: C
scheme.explanation: An ATM needs an immediate, interactive answer.

questions.title: Queuing output
questions.text: State the term for putting output for a slow device, such as a printer, into a queue on disk so the processor can continue with the next job.

scheme.mark_scheme: spooling (1)
scheme.explanation: Spooling (Simultaneous Peripheral Operations On-Line).

questions.title: Job instructions
questions.text: Batch jobs are submitted with instructions written in advance in a **job control language**. State the usual abbreviation for job control language.

scheme.mark_scheme: JCL (1)
scheme.explanation: JCL — e.g. on IBM mainframes.

questions.title: Interaction in batch
questions.text: In batch processing the user is asked for input while each job runs.

scheme.mark_scheme: False.
scheme.explanation: Batch jobs run without user interaction; all data and instructions are prepared in advance.

questions.title: Real-time systems in a car
questions.text: A new electric car has an **airbag controller**, **anti-lock brakes (ABS)**, a **navigation screen** and a **music player**. Each is controlled by an embedded computer.

parts.title: Define RTOS
parts.text: Describe a **real-time operating system**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- processes data / responds to inputs within a guaranteed time limit / deadline (1)
- in order to monitor / control a physical process as it happens / output affects the next input (feedback) (1)
scheme.model_answer: An OS that processes inputs from sensors and responds within a strict, guaranteed time limit, so that it can control a physical process such as inflating an airbag as events happen.

parts.title: Hard real-time
parts.text: Explain why the airbag controller must be a **hard** real-time system.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- the airbag must inflate within a strict deadline (milliseconds after the crash is sensed) (1)
- a late response is a failure / is useless / could injure or kill the driver (1)
scheme.model_answer: The airbag must inflate within a few milliseconds of the crash sensor's signal; if it is late it is useless and the driver could be seriously injured, so missing a deadline counts as a system failure.

parts.title: Features
parts.text: Describe **two** features of a real-time operating system that make sure the airbag inflates in time.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Two features, each identified (1) and described in context (1):
- priority-based pre-emptive scheduling (1) — the crash-detection task has the highest priority and interrupts any other task immediately (1)
- fast interrupt handling / low interrupt latency (1) — the crash sensor's signal is handled almost at once (1)
- deterministic / predictable response time (1) — the worst-case time is known, so the deadline can be guaranteed (1)
- continuous monitoring of sensors (1) — the deceleration sensor is read constantly (1)
- reliability / fault tolerance / redundancy (1) — works every time / backup sensors (1)
scheme.model_answer: Pre-emptive priority scheduling: the crash-detection task has the highest priority, so it interrupts the music or display task immediately. Deterministic response: the maximum time to react is known and tested, so the airbag is guaranteed to inflate within its deadline.

parts.title: Hard or soft
parts.text: Tick (✓) **one** box in each row.

prefill: Anti-lock brakes (ABS)
Navigation screen updating the map

scheme.mark_scheme: ABS brakes – hard (1); navigation screen updates – soft (1)
scheme.model_answer: ABS brakes: hard real-time. Navigation screen: soft real-time.

questions.title: A college network
questions.text: A college has **1 200 students** and **90 staff**. All computers are connected to servers that run a **network operating system (NOS)**. Teachers keep exam papers in a folder on the server.

parts.title: Describe NOS
parts.text: Describe a **network operating system**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- an OS (usually on a server) that manages a network / connected computers (1)
- controls shared resources (files, printers, software) and the users who access them / users, security, access (1)

points.criterion: Manages a network / runs on server

scheme.model_answer: An operating system running on the college's servers that manages the network: it controls the users and their access to shared resources such as files, printers and software.

parts.title: Functions
parts.text: State **three** functions of the NOS, other than managing user accounts.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any three (1 each): file sharing / central storage; printer sharing / print queues; security / firewall / encryption; audit log / monitoring; central backup; software updates / installation; remote administration; network services (DHCP, DNS, e-mail)
scheme.model_answer: 1 Shared printers with print queues. 2 Central backup of all files. 3 Audit logs of who accessed which file.

parts.title: Protecting the exam folder
parts.text: Describe how the NOS uses **user accounts** to stop students opening the exam folder.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- each user has an account (user name + password) / is placed in a group, e.g. Students, Teachers (1)
- at log-in the NOS authenticates the user / checks the user name and password (1)
- the NOS checks the access rights of the account / group (authorisation): students' group has no access to the exam folder, teachers have read/write (1)
(also accept: attempts recorded in an audit log)
scheme.model_answer: Every student has an account in the Students group. When they log in, the NOS authenticates their user name and password. It then checks the group's access rights: the Students group has 'no access' to the exam folder, so the NOS refuses to open it, while the Teachers group has read/write rights.

parts.title: Two security terms
parts.text: Draw lines to match each term to its meaning.

right.text: Deciding which resources the user may access
Copying the user's files to a backup

scheme.mark_scheme: Authentication – checking who the user is (1); Authorisation – deciding which resources the user may access (1)
scheme.model_answer: Authentication: checking who the user is. Authorisation: deciding which resources the user may access.

questions.title: Mobile phone billing
questions.text: A mobile operator in Kazakhstan has **3 million** customers. Records of every call, SMS and data session are stored during the month, and the bills are produced by **batch processing** on the last night of the month.

parts.title: Describe batch
parts.text: Describe a **batch processing** operating system.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- jobs with similar requirements are grouped (into batches) and run one after another (1)
- automatically, without user interaction / at a scheduled time / data collected over a period and processed together (1)

points.criterion: Similar jobs grouped and run in sequence
No interaction / scheduled / data collected over a period

scheme.model_answer: An OS that groups similar jobs into batches and runs them one after another automatically, without any user interaction, usually at a scheduled time after the data has been collected over a period.

parts.title: Steps
parts.text: Describe how the monthly bills are produced, from collecting the call records to printing the bills.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Any four (1 each):
- call / SMS / data records are collected during the month in a transaction file
- the records are sorted (e.g. by customer number) to match the master file
- the billing job is submitted / placed in a job queue with instructions (JCL / script)
- the job runs at a scheduled time / at night / off-peak, without an operator / user interaction
- each customer's records are matched with the master file (tariff, address) and the bill is calculated
- bills are spooled to printers / files; a new master file is created
scheme.model_answer: During the month all call records are stored in a transaction file. On the last day they are sorted by customer number. The billing job is placed in the job queue to run at night. The OS runs it automatically, matching each customer's records with the master file to calculate the bill, and the bills are spooled to the printers.

parts.title: Advantage and disadvantage
parts.text: Give **one** advantage and **one** disadvantage to the operator of using batch processing for billing.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Advantage (1): processes millions of similar records efficiently / runs at night when the computers are not busy / no operator needed / consistent results.
Disadvantage (1): bills / results are delayed until the batch runs / errors found only after the whole batch has run / cannot change jobs while running.
scheme.model_answer: Advantage: 3 million bills are produced efficiently overnight when the servers are not busy, with no operator. Disadvantage: an error in the tariff is found only after all the bills have been produced.

parts.title: Suitable for batch?
parts.text: Tick (✓) **one** box in each row to show whether the task is suitable for batch processing.

prefill: E-mailing monthly statements to all customers
Topping up a customer's balance at a payment kiosk

scheme.mark_scheme: Monthly statements – suitable (1); topping up the balance at a kiosk – not suitable (1)
scheme.model_answer: Monthly statements e-mailed to customers: suitable. Topping up the balance at a kiosk: not suitable (needs an immediate response).

questions.title: Choosing operating systems
questions.text: A city transport company runs **traffic lights**, an **office** where 300 staff share files and printers, and a system that calculates **fares** from passengers' travel-card taps every night.

parts.title: Choose the type
parts.text: Tick (✓) the most suitable type of operating system for each system.

prefill: Traffic lights that react to sensors
Office of 300 staff sharing files and printers
Calculating all fares from travel-card taps each night

scheme.mark_scheme: Traffic lights – real-time (1); office – network (1); nightly fares – batch (1)
scheme.model_answer: Traffic lights: real-time. Office: network. Nightly fares: batch.

parts.title: Compare RTOS and batch
parts.text: Compare a **real-time** operating system with a **batch processing** operating system.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Two comparisons, each needs both sides (2 + 2):
- response: RTOS responds immediately / within a guaranteed deadline (1); batch results are delayed until the batch is run (1)
- interaction / input: RTOS reacts continuously to sensor inputs / events (1); batch has no interaction, data collected in advance and processed together (1)
- scheduling: RTOS uses priority-based pre-emptive scheduling (1); batch runs jobs one after another from a queue at a scheduled time (1)
- data: RTOS processes each input as it arrives (1); batch processes large volumes of similar data at once (1)
scheme.model_answer: A real-time OS responds to each input within a guaranteed deadline, whereas a batch OS produces results only when the whole batch has been run later. A real-time OS reacts continuously to events from sensors, but a batch OS needs no interaction: the data is collected in advance and processed together at a scheduled time.

parts.title: Client–server for the office
parts.text: The office could use a peer-to-peer network or a client–server network with a NOS. Explain why a client–server network with a NOS is more suitable for the 300 staff.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Any three (1 each), linked to the office:
- central management of 300 user accounts / access rights from one place
- better security: rights set centrally, authentication at log-in, audit logs
- central / automatic backup of everyone's files
- shared printers and files managed centrally / print queues
- staff can log in on any computer and see their files
- peer-to-peer is only suitable for small networks; with 300 users it would be hard to manage / insecure
scheme.model_answer: With 300 staff, the administrator can manage all accounts and access rights from the server instead of on each PC. The NOS authenticates every user and keeps audit logs, so security is stronger, and all files are backed up centrally every night. Peer-to-peer is only practical for a few computers.

questions.title: Intensive care unit
questions.text: A hospital in Karaganda is equipping its **intensive care unit**. Each bed has a **ventilator** that helps the patient breathe and a **patient monitor** that measures heart rate and blood oxygen and shows them on a screen. Both are controlled by a **real-time operating system (RTOS)**. The hospital also runs a **video consultation** service so that doctors in other cities can see patients.

parts.title: Meaning of real-time
parts.text: Explain what is meant by **real-time** in a real-time operating system.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- the system processes inputs and responds within a guaranteed / strict time limit / deadline (1)
- it works at the speed of the real-world process it controls / a result is only correct if it is produced on time (not simply "very fast") (1)

points.criterion: Keeps pace with the real-world process / correct only if on time

scheme.model_answer: Real-time means the system processes each input and responds within a guaranteed deadline, keeping pace with the physical process it controls; a result is only correct if it is produced on time, so being predictable matters more than being fast.

parts.title: Interrupts and priorities
parts.text: The monitor is updating its screen when the oxygen sensor detects that the patient's blood oxygen has fallen below a safe level. Describe how the RTOS uses **interrupts** and **priorities** to respond.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- the oxygen sensor sends an interrupt (signal) to the processor (1)
- the alarm / ventilator task has a higher priority than the screen-update task (1)
- the RTOS pre-empts / pauses the screen task, saving its state (1)
- the high-priority task runs immediately (sounds the alarm / adjusts the ventilator) within the deadline, then the screen task is resumed (1)

points.criterion: Alarm / ventilator task has higher priority
Urgent task runs at once, display resumed after

scheme.model_answer: The oxygen sensor sends an interrupt to the processor. The task that raises the alarm and adjusts the ventilator has a higher priority than the screen-update task, so the RTOS pre-empts the screen task and saves its state. The urgent task runs immediately and finishes within its deadline; afterwards the RTOS resumes the screen update where it stopped.

parts.title: Hard and soft
parts.text: Explain why the ventilator is a **hard** real-time system but the video consultation service is a **soft** real-time system.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- ventilator: a missed deadline is a system failure / could harm or kill the patient (1)
- video consultation: a missed deadline only lowers quality (frozen picture, delayed sound) and the system keeps working (1)

points.criterion: Ventilator — missed deadline is dangerous / failure
Video — missed deadline only reduces quality

scheme.model_answer: If the ventilator misses a deadline the patient may not get air, which is a dangerous failure, so every deadline must be guaranteed. If the video call misses a deadline the picture freezes or the sound is delayed, which lowers quality but is not dangerous.

parts.title: Classify the systems
parts.text: Tick (✓) **one** box in each row.

prefill: Insulin pump that injects a dose when blood sugar is high
Screen in the waiting room streaming health videos

scheme.mark_scheme: Insulin pump – hard (1); streaming health videos – soft (1)
scheme.model_answer: Insulin pump: hard real-time. Streaming videos: soft real-time.

questions.title: Welding robot
questions.text: A factory in Pavlodar uses **welding robots** to join steel parts. Each robot has sensors that measure the **position** of its arm and the **temperature** of the weld, and motors that move the arm. The robots are controlled by an RTOS. A manager suggests saving money by controlling the robots from ordinary office PCs running a **general-purpose operating system** such as Windows.

parts.title: Feedback loop
parts.text: Describe how the RTOS uses **feedback** to control the position of the robot arm.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- sensors measure the arm's position continuously and send the readings to the computer (1)
- the control program compares the reading with the required position (1)
- it sends a signal to the actuators / motors to correct the position, and the new position is measured again — the output affects the next input (loop repeats) (1)
scheme.model_answer: Position sensors measure where the arm is many times a second and send the readings to the RTOS. The control program compares each reading with the position the arm should be in. If they differ, it sends a signal to the motors to move the arm; the new position is then measured again, so the output of the system affects its next input in a continuous loop.

parts.title: Why not a general-purpose OS
parts.text: Explain **two** reasons why a general-purpose operating system is **not** suitable for controlling the welding robots.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Two reasons, each identified (1) + explained in context (1):
- not deterministic / response time varies with the load (1) → the robot may react too late and weld in the wrong place / damage the part (1)
- uses time-sharing / fairness between programs, not strict priority pre-emption (1) → the urgent control task may have to wait behind other programs (1)
- large, needs updates and restarts / less reliable (1) → the robot could stop in the middle of a weld / production line stops (1)
- higher interrupt latency (1) → a dangerous temperature reading is not handled at once (1)
scheme.model_answer: A general-purpose OS is not deterministic: its response time depends on how busy the PC is, so the arm could move too late and weld in the wrong place. It also shares processor time fairly between many programs instead of always running the most urgent task first, so the control task might wait behind an update or another program while the weld overheats.

parts.title: Another feature
parts.text: State **one** other feature of an RTOS that makes it suitable for the factory robots.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any one (1): high reliability / fault tolerance / runs for years without restarting; redundant (duplicated) hardware; small and efficient / embedded in ROM or flash; minimal user interface; fast interrupt handling / low interrupt latency
scheme.model_answer: It is highly reliable and fault tolerant, so it can run for years without being restarted.

questions.title: IT company network
questions.text: **DalaSoft**, a software company in Astana, has **150 employees** in three departments: Developers, Accounts and HR. Every computer is connected to a server that runs a **network operating system (NOS)**. Salaries are kept in the shared folder **\\Finance** and staff records in **\\HR**.

parts.title: Authentication and authorisation
parts.text: Explain the difference between **authentication** and **authorisation** when an employee of DalaSoft opens the \\Finance folder.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- authentication: the NOS checks who the employee is, e.g. user name and password / 2FA, at log-in (1)
- authorisation: the NOS then checks the access rights of the account / group to decide whether this employee may open / change \\Finance (1)

points.criterion: Authorisation — rights to the folder checked

scheme.model_answer: Authentication checks who the employee is: at log-in the NOS compares the user name and password with its account database. Authorisation then decides what that employee may do: the NOS checks the access rights of the account and its groups and only lets an Accounts employee open \\Finance.

parts.title: Groups
parts.text: A new accountant joins DalaSoft. Describe how the network administrator uses the NOS so that the accountant can open \\Finance but **not** \\HR.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- creates a user account with a user name and (initial) password / password policy (1)
- adds the account to the Accounts group (1)
- the Accounts group already has read / write rights to \\Finance and no access to \\HR, so the new user gets the correct rights automatically / without setting each folder (1)

points.criterion: Rights come from the group: Finance yes, HR no

scheme.model_answer: The administrator creates an account for the accountant with a user name and a temporary password that must be changed at first log-in. The account is added to the Accounts group. That group already has read/write rights to \\Finance and no access to \\HR, so the new accountant automatically gets exactly the right access.

parts.title: Another function
parts.text: Describe **one** other function of the NOS, apart from managing user accounts, and how it benefits DalaSoft.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Function (1) + benefit in context (1), e.g.:
- central backup of shared folders (1) → code / salary files can be restored if a computer fails (1)
- audit log of who accessed what (1) → the company can see who opened staff records in \\HR (1)
- printer sharing / print queues (1) → fewer printers to buy (1)
- pushing software updates / installing software on all clients (1) → developers all use the same, secure versions (1)
- security: firewall / encryption (1) → protects source code from outsiders (1)
scheme.model_answer: The NOS backs up all shared folders to the server every night, so if a developer's computer breaks or a file is deleted, the company's code and salary data can be restored.

questions.title: National testing centre
questions.text: A national testing centre marks the multiple-choice answer sheets of **150 000** school leavers. During the day the sheets are scanned and the answers are stored in a **transaction file**. Each night a **batch processing** operating system matches the answers with the **master file** of candidates (ID, name, school), calculates the scores and prints a results certificate for every candidate.

parts.title: Sorting the transaction file
parts.text: Explain why the transaction file is **sorted** before it is processed.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- it is sorted by the key field (candidate ID) into the same order as the master file (1)
- so each master record can be matched with its transactions in one pass / read once in sequence, without searching (faster, efficient) (1)

points.criterion: Same key order as master file
Matching in one pass without searching

scheme.model_answer: The transaction file is sorted by candidate ID, the same key field as the master file. The OS can then read both files once from start to end and match each candidate with their answers in one pass, without searching, which is much faster for 150 000 records.

parts.title: Running the job
parts.text: Describe how the batch processing OS runs the marking job each night **without an operator**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- the job is written in advance in a job control language / script stating which program, which files and what to do on an error (1)
- it is placed in a job queue / scheduled, and the OS starts it automatically at the set time (off-peak) and runs the jobs one after another with no user interaction (1)

points.criterion: Job queue, scheduled automatic start, one after another

scheme.model_answer: The marking job is written in advance in a job control language that tells the OS which program to run, which files to use and what to do if an error occurs. The job waits in the job queue and at the scheduled time at night the OS starts it automatically and runs each job in turn with no one at the computer.

parts.title: Spooling
parts.text: The certificates are **spooled** to the printers. Explain what spooling is and why it is useful here.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- output for the slow printer is stored in a queue on disk (1)
- so the processor does not wait for the printer and can carry on with the next job / candidates while the printers work through the queue (1)

points.criterion: Output queued on disk for the printer

scheme.model_answer: Spooling puts each certificate into a print queue on disk instead of sending it straight to the slow printer. The processor can then continue marking the next candidates while the printers work through the queue.

parts.title: A disadvantage
parts.text: Explain **one** disadvantage of using batch processing for the testing centre.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Disadvantage (1) + explained in context (1), e.g.:
- errors are found only after the whole batch has run (1) → e.g. a wrongly scanned set of sheets or a wrong answer key means the whole night's run must be repeated (1)
- results are delayed / not available immediately (1) → candidates must wait until the next day for their score (1)
- the job cannot be changed / no interaction while it runs (1) → a mistake noticed at midnight cannot be fixed until the batch ends (1)
scheme.model_answer: Errors are found only after the whole batch has run: if the answer key loaded that night is wrong, all 150 000 scores are wrong and the whole batch has to be run again.

blocks.content: Operating systems are designed for different **workloads**. A laptop OS is built for **one user running many programs** with good average speed. Other systems must **react within a fixed time**, **serve hundreds of users over a network**, or **process millions of records without anyone watching** — each needs a different type of OS.

rows: **Process large volumes of similar jobs efficiently**
Little or none — sensors and actuators
Many users at once over the network
Servers in schools, offices, data centres

blocks.content: An operating system that **processes data and responds to events within a strict, guaranteed time limit (deadline)**, so that it can **monitor and control** a physical process as it happens. A result is only correct if it is produced **on time**.

The word "real-time" does not mean "very fast". It means that the computer works **at the speed of the real world** it controls. A real-time system is connected to the physical world through **sensors** (inputs such as temperature probes, pressure sensors, wheel-speed sensors) and **actuators** (outputs such as motors, valves, heaters and alarms). The OS reads the sensors, the control program compares the readings with set values, and the OS sends signals to the actuators — and then the cycle starts again. Because each output changes the physical process, and the sensors then measure that change, this is called a **feedback loop**. For a feedback loop to be safe, every pass through it must finish before the physical process has changed too much: an airbag must inflate within about 30 milliseconds of a crash, long before the passenger hits the steering wheel. If the response came later, a perfectly correct calculation would still be useless. That is why, for an RTOS, **timing is part of correctness**.

items.title: Key features of an RTOS
items.content:
- **Deterministic** — the time to respond to an event is **predictable** and always within the deadline.
- **Priority-based pre-emptive scheduling** — the most urgent task **interrupts** lower-priority tasks immediately.
- **Fast interrupt handling** — very low **interrupt latency**.
- **Continuous monitoring** of sensors with **feedback** to actuators.
- **High reliability / fault tolerance** — runs for years without restarting; often duplicated (redundant) hardware.
- **Small and efficient** — stored in ROM / flash of an **embedded** device; little or no user interface.

items.title: Where RTOSs are used
items.content:
- Car **airbags** and **anti-lock brakes (ABS)**.
- **Pacemakers** and hospital patient monitors.
- Aircraft **autopilot** and flight control.
- **Industrial robots**, traffic lights, greenhouse and nuclear-plant control.
- Online games and video calls (soft real-time).

blocks.content: A **signal** from hardware (e.g. a sensor) or software that tells the processor an event **needs attention now**; the OS pauses the current task and runs the task that handles the event.

How does an RTOS make sure the most important work is always done on time? The control software is divided into separate **tasks**, and the designers give each task a **priority** that reflects how urgent it is: the brake-control task in a car has a higher priority than the task that updates the dashboard display. When a sensor detects an event, it sends an **interrupt**. The RTOS immediately saves the state of the task that is running, looks at the priorities, and if the new task is more urgent it **pre-empts** (takes the processor away from) the current task and starts the urgent one. When the urgent task finishes, the interrupted task continues from where it stopped. The time between the interrupt and the start of the handling task is called the **interrupt latency**, and an RTOS keeps it very short and, above all, **bounded** — it never exceeds a known maximum. A general-purpose OS like Windows also uses interrupts, but it shares processor time fairly between many programs and may pause for background work such as updates or memory management, so its worst-case response time cannot be guaranteed. Being deterministic also explains why RTOSs are **small**: fewer features mean fewer unpredictable delays and less to go wrong, which is also why they can run reliably for years inside an embedded device.

blocks.content:
Sensors measure **temperature** and **humidity** every second.
1. The reading 32 °C arrives as an **interrupt** from the temperature sensor.
2. The RTOS runs the **ventilation task** at once, because it has a higher priority than updating the display.
3. The task decides that 32 °C is above the 30 °C limit and opens the windows **within 2 seconds** (the deadline).
4. If the **fire sensor** triggers, the alarm task has the **highest priority** and interrupts every other task immediately.
5. The new temperature is measured again — the **feedback loop** continues day and night.

- Saying an RTOS is just "very fast" — the key idea is a **guaranteed deadline** (predictability). A slow response that is always on time is fine.
- Mixing up hard and soft: a **video call** is soft real-time, not hard.
- Calling any app that shows live data (e.g. weather) a real-time OS — the OS must **control** something within a deadline.

An operating system that **manages a network** of computers: its **shared resources** — files, printers, applications, Internet access — and the **users** who access them. It usually runs on a **server**, and client computers connect to it.

A stand-alone OS looks after one computer: its own files, its own printer, its own users. As soon as an organisation has dozens or hundreds of computers, managing each one separately becomes impossible — every password, every folder permission and every backup would have to be set up machine by machine. A network operating system solves this by **centralising** control. In a **client–server** network, the NOS runs on one or more powerful **servers**. The client computers (pupils' PCs, teachers' laptops) run an ordinary OS, but when a user logs in, the client sends the user name and password to the server, and the server decides whether the user may log in and what they may use. Shared files are stored on the server's disks, shared printers are managed through the server's print queues, and the server keeps a single database of all users and groups (in Windows Server this is called **Active Directory**).

The two key ideas are **authentication** and **authorisation**. Authentication answers the question "**who are you?**" — the NOS checks the user name and password (and sometimes a second factor such as a code on a phone) against its account database. Authorisation answers "**what are you allowed to do?**" — once the user is known, the NOS checks the **access rights** of the account and of every group it belongs to, and allows only the permitted actions on each folder, file or printer. Giving rights to **groups** instead of individual users is what makes a NOS practical: when a new pupil joins grade 12, the administrator only adds the account to the "Grade 12" group, and the pupil immediately gets the right access to every resource. Because every access passes through the server, the NOS can also **log** it, which supports security and accountability.
Checking the **identity** of a user ("who are you?"), e.g. by user name and password or two-factor authentication, before allowing log-in.
Deciding **what an authenticated user may access and do** ("what are you allowed to do?"), using the access rights of the account and its groups.

blocks.caption: A NOS on a server manages users and shared resources

items.title: Functions of a NOS
items.content:
- **User account management** — creates accounts and **groups**, sets **passwords** and **password policies**.
- **Authentication** — checks **who** the user is (user name + password, 2FA).
- **Authorisation** — gives each account **access rights** to resources (read, write, no access).
- **File and printer sharing** — central storage, home folders, **print queues**.
- **Security** — firewall, encryption, **audit logs** of who accessed what.
- **Centralised backup** and **software updates** for all clients.
- **Remote administration** and network services — DHCP, DNS, e-mail.
- Supports **many users at the same time**.

items.title: Why organisations use one
items.content:
- One administrator controls the whole network from **one place**.
- Users can **log in on any computer** and see their own files.
- Data is **backed up centrally** and access is **controlled**.
- Expensive resources (printers, software licences) are **shared**.

blocks.title: How a NOS manages user accounts
items: The administrator creates an **account** for each user and adds it to **groups** (e.g. Teachers, Grade 12).
Access rights are given to **groups**, so a new pupil gets the right access just by joining a group.
When a user **logs in**, the NOS checks the user name and password — **authentication**.
The NOS checks the rights of the account and its groups — **authorisation**.
The user can open only the folders and printers they are allowed to use; each access may be **logged**.
When a user leaves, the administrator **disables** the account in one place.

blocks.title: Worked example: a clinic with 40 staff
blocks.content:
A clinic in Shymkent installs a server with a NOS.
- Doctors, nurses and receptionists each have an **account** in a **group**.
- Patient records are in a shared folder: doctors **read / write**, receptionists **read** only the appointments folder.
- Every night the NOS **backs up** the shared folders; the **audit log** shows who opened each patient file.
- A nurse can log in at **any** computer in the clinic and see their own documents.

- Describing a NOS as "an OS for the Internet" — it **manages users and shared resources** on a network.
- Confusing **authentication** (who are you?) with **authorisation** (what may you access?).
- Saying a NOS is the same as a **multi-user** OS — a NOS is usually multi-user, but its focus is **managing the network's resources**.

An operating system that **groups jobs with similar requirements into batches** and **runs them one after another automatically, without user interaction**, usually at a **scheduled time**. The data is **collected over a period** and processed **together**.

Batch processing is the oldest way of running a computer, and it is still used today wherever **huge amounts of similar data** must be processed. The idea is simple: instead of a person sitting at the computer and processing each item as it arrives, the items are **collected** for a period (a day, a week, a month) and then processed **all at once** by a program that needs no human help. Because the computer does the same operation on every record, it can work at full speed without waiting for anyone to type or click, so the total processing is very **efficient**.

A batch system typically works with two files. The **master file** holds the permanent data, such as each customer's name, address, tariff and balance, sorted by a key field such as the customer number. The **transaction file** holds the changes collected during the period, such as each meter reading or each card payment. Before processing, the transaction file is **sorted into the same order** as the master file; the program can then read both files once from start to end, match each transaction with its master record, update it and write a **new master file**. This single sequential pass is what makes batch processing so fast for very large volumes.

The jobs themselves are described in advance in a **job control language (JCL)** or a script, which tells the OS which program to run, which files to use and what to do if an error occurs. The batch OS holds the submitted jobs in a **job queue**, chooses the order in which they run (for example by priority or by the resources they need), starts each job automatically when the previous one finishes, and **spools** the output so that slow printers do not hold up the processor. Jobs are usually scheduled for **off-peak** times such as the night, when the computer is not needed by interactive users.

blocks.caption: Batch processing: collect, sort, queue, run

blocks.title: How batch processing works
items: Jobs (programs + their data) are **submitted** with instructions written in advance — a **job control language (JCL)** or a script.
Jobs are placed in a **job queue** and **grouped** with similar jobs.
Input data is often **sorted** first (e.g. by customer number) so it is in the same order as the **master file**.
At the scheduled time (often **at night**, off-peak), the OS runs the jobs **one by one**, with no operator.
Output (bills, payslips, reports) is **spooled** to printers or files, and a **new master file** is produced.

blocks.content: Putting output for a slow device (such as a printer) into a **queue on disk**, so that the processor can carry on with the next job while the device works through the queue.

items.title: Features
items.content:
- Jobs with similar requirements are **batched together** and run as a group.
- Data is **collected over a defined period** and processed as one pack.
- **No interaction** with users while the jobs run.
- **Sorting** before processing; **scheduling** at off-peak times.
- **Spooling** of output for slow devices.

items.title: Uses
items.content:
- **Payroll** at the end of each month.
- **Utility bills** (electricity, water, gas) and **bank statements**.
- End-of-day processing of **card payments**.
- **Exam results**, census data, overnight **backups** and reports.

blocks.title: Batch processing — advantages and disadvantages
rows: **Efficient** for very large volumes of similar data
Uses the computer at **off-peak** times (e.g. at night)
Errors may be found only **after** the whole batch has run
Jobs cannot be changed once they are running
Not suitable for interactive or urgent tasks

blocks.title: Worked example: electricity bills
blocks.content:
An energy company in Almaty has **400 000** customers.
1. Smart meters send readings all month; they are stored in a **transaction file**.
2. On the last day, the readings are **sorted** by customer ID.
3. A **job** is queued to run at 01:00 with the JCL instructions.
4. The OS processes every customer **without interaction**, matching each reading with the **master file** (tariff, address).
5. 400 000 bills are **spooled** to the printers and a new master file is saved. No customer needs their bill instantly, so the delay does not matter.

Exam questions often describe a situation and ask you to **identify** the most suitable type of operating system and **justify** your choice. Ask three questions about the scenario. First, **does it control a physical process where a late response is a failure?** If yes, it needs a real-time OS — and if a missed deadline could harm people or equipment, it is hard real-time. Second, **do many users need to share files, printers or applications, with central control of security?** That points to a network OS on a server. Third, **is there a large volume of similar data that can wait and be processed together without anyone watching?** That is batch processing. Always link the reason to a detail **in the scenario** ("the 400 000 bills are not needed immediately, so they can be processed overnight"), because a general definition alone usually earns only one mark. Remember that a real organisation often uses all three types: a bank runs a NOS for its office staff, an RTOS inside its cash machines' hardware and batch jobs at night to process the day's card payments.

blocks.content:
- Saying users can interact with batch jobs while they run — batch processing runs **without** interaction.
- Choosing batch for anything that needs an **immediate** answer (e.g. a cash machine checking a balance).
- Forgetting the **delay**: "efficient" is an advantage only when results are **not** needed at once.

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Describe a real-time operating system. [2]**
It processes inputs and responds **within a guaranteed time limit / deadline** (1), so that it can **monitor and control a physical process** as it happens, e.g. an airbag or a factory robot (1).

**Q: Explain why a pacemaker needs a hard real-time operating system. [2]**
The pacemaker must react to the heart's signals **within a strict deadline** (1); a late response could **endanger the patient's life**, so a missed deadline is a failure (1).

**Q: State two functions of a network operating system. [2]**
Any two: managing **user accounts** and groups (1); **authentication** / **access rights** (1); file and printer sharing; central backup; audit logs; software updates.

**Q: Describe how a NOS controls which files a pupil can open. [3]**
The pupil has an **account** in a **group** created by the administrator (1). At log-in the NOS **authenticates** the user name and password (1). It then checks the **access rights** of the account / group and allows only the permitted folders (1).

**Q: Explain why batch processing is suitable for producing monthly payslips. [2]**
There is a **large volume of similar jobs** (one for each employee) that can be processed together (1); payslips are **not needed immediately**, so they can be run **at night / off-peak without an operator** (1).

**Q: State one disadvantage of batch processing. [1]**
Results are **delayed** / errors are found only after the batch has run / no interaction is possible (1).

- Giving an **example** only ("an airbag") when the question says **describe** — first say what the OS does (deadline, control), then give the example.
- Writing "it is faster" for any OS type — explain **what** it does differently.
- In scenario questions, naming the type without a **reason linked to the scenario**.
